Does mixing drinks make you get drunk faster like many people think? and why?
Dunno if you it make ppl drunk faster but for sure it can make you puke more :P

All that matters is BAC.

BAC is determined, generally, by the amount of alcohol you've consumed per period of time.

That is, the higher your rate of alcohol consumption, the quicker your BAC will rise.

It doesn't matter what you've mixed with the alcohol (beer, soda, water, juice), or whether you're mixing it with different things from drink to drink.

There might be a psycho-social explanation in that the kind of circumstances where you mix drinks a lot are also the ones where you drink more and faster and exhibit less constrained behaviour, basically wild parties.
Mixed drinks may enable faster consumption, but this is the right answer.

Does the body process all alcohol equally though? (genuinely asking)

It seems possible that certain types of alcohol could be broken down and passed through the body at different rates and perhaps mixing drinks in certain ways could lead to an increase in BAC quicker. If it does I doubt it's all that significant though and chances are the reason people really believe this is simply that when they're mixing drinks they generally are drinking more than usual and so of course are ending up drunker. Probably also less accurately tracking how much they've actually had since they're switching about.

All alcohol you get drunk on is ethanol.

There are several factors that determine how quickly it gets in to the bloodstream, including, but not limited to: gender, BMI, heart rate, activity level, stomach contents, and consumption method.

For examples of the last variable, taking alcohol rectally or intravenously will result in a sharper rise in BAC.

The stomach content part is what plays in to 40% vodka not necessarily being absorbed at the same rate as 40% tequilla, or, vodka/milk not being absorbed as quickly as vodka/water, but, as you speculated, this is not as significant a factor as the others.
I don't think so. But if you're mixing drinks you're probably knocking them back like there's no tomorrow, so the chances of getting drunk are more likely.

Coming from another angle, if you're talking about the "Liquor before beer, in the clean, beer before liquor never sicker" saying as your 'mixing drinks' (it's what came to my mind before thinking of having a vodka drink, then a rum drink, then a whiskey drink)... Then there is Some truth to the saying, but it has to do with the rate of absorption of the alcohol.

Beer has a very delayed rate of absorption... meaning, it takes awhile for the body to process the liquid and for you to show side effects. Distilled alcohol doesn't have that delay, it's much more immediate (though, there is still a delay). So if you're drinking lots of beer, feel fine after 8~10 and then start in on the distilled spirits, you're lining yourself up for a larger "hit" of alcohol... On the other hand, if you're drinking spirits and switch to beer, there's a lag between the last infusion of alcohol to your body with the spirits and the first from the beer, which allows the liver to do some work first.

I'm not sure I've ever heard of or seen anyone do beer and/or spirits with wine, but it'll sorta be a similar deal (12oz of wine being about like 24~36oz of beer for alcoholic content and less delay than beer, but still more than spirits).

From my experience as a bartender and going through lots of TIPS certification classes, BAC and alcohol tolerance are the two biggest factors with how drunk and how fast. How much alcohol you consume in how much time is whats most important - doesn't really matter what the alcohol is or how it's mixed. Beer is usually around 12-16% alcohol, liquor is ~40%. If you mix a shot of something, then add just as much of a mixer that's non alcoholic (2oz Vodka + 2oz Soda + Ice) you drop the alcohol content of that drink down to ~20%. As ice melts, it dilutes the drink even further. How many you drink in a given amount of time - that's the deciding factor.

And this is a bit off topic, but I've seen people with a relatively low BAC tripping over themselves, and people with a relatively high BAC pass an inebriation test with ease. Lots of people like to say "Oh I can drink Vodka (light liquor), but Whiskey (dark liquor) gives me hangovers, or vice-versa - or wine gives me a headache but beer is fine. This is all heresy. This is really all a matter of how hydrated you are when you drink. If a person drinks vodka sodas all night, of course they'll wake up feeling much better than the person that drank the same amount of whiskey sours. The person drinking sodas is consuming more water per drink than the other person. If you want to save yourself from a hangover, drink water/gatorade/coconut water while your drinking.
